title: Championship play-offs expanded: Why EFL is increasing routes into Premier League
content:
There will be more routes to reach the Premier League from next season after an English Football League (EFL) vote was passed to expand the Championship play-offs from four teams to six.

The team finishing eighth in the Championship will get the chance to win promotion to the top flight under the expanded play-off structure from 2026-27, the EFL confirmed in a statement on Thursday.

The current system, in place since 1988-89, has seen four clubs finishing between third and sixth progress to a knock-out tournament to claim the third promotion slot, but that format will now be widened to include those finishing in seventh and eighth.

A vote of all 72 EFL clubs was held at an extraordinary general meeting (EGM) on Thursday to approve the changes which will be introduced from next season.

The new format will broadly mirror the National League play-off system, where the two highest finishers will get a bye through the first stage. It is expected that fifth will play eighth and sixth will play seventh, with the two winners progressing to face those that ended in third and fourth.

The remainder of the play-offs would then replicate the existing programme, with two semi-finals played over two legs leading to a final at Wembley. That fixture has long been described as football’s most valuable game, bringing a guaranteed revenue uplift of £180million over three years.

The new proposals are designed to widen the excitement in the closing weeks of the Championship season and reduce the number of dead rubber contests.

The second-tier play-offs have involved four teams since their introduction in 1987 — initially three teams from the second division plus the team that finished one place above the relegation zone in the top flight. This was changed to involve the teams from third to sixth in the second tier from the 1988-89 season, and the final was changed from a two-legged affair to a one-off game the following year.

The Athletic reported in September that the EFL was considering a plan to add an eliminator round to the Championship play-offs, and the Football Association’s board had given its approval for a vote at the end of last year, paving the way for the EFL’s 72 clubs to vote through the changes when meeting at The Belfry on Thursday. The proposals required a straight majority of at least 13 Championship clubs and 37 EFL clubs overall to pass.

EFL Chief Executive, Trevor Birch, said: “Since their introduction in 1986-87, the play-offs have become a highlight of the domestic football calendar, capturing the drama, suspense and jeopardy that make the EFL so special.

“Following several months of discussion with Clubs and other stakeholders, we are confident this change will further strengthen the Championship as a competition and give more Clubs and their supporters a genuine opportunity of achieving promotion.”

This season’s play-offs will remain a four-team contest, with Wrexham currently the team in sixth, below Ipswich Town (3rd), Millwall (4th), and Hull City (5th). Leagues One and Two will not immediately change to a six-team play-off format, but success in the Championship could eventually lead to them expanding their own end-of-season programmes.

The means of escaping the Championship have been unchanged for a generation. Ever since 1988-89, there have been two automatic promotion places and a third slot going to one of the clubs finishing between third and sixth.

That play-off format has created untold drama as clubs have battled to reach the Premier League, but the EFL has opted for more.

Expanding the Championship play-offs will hand new opportunities to those finishing in seventh and eighth. Their route will be the toughest, bringing away games at higher-ranked clubs, but the additional fixtures are designed to heighten drama and interest around English football’s second tier.

There will be obvious concerns. Last season saw Millwall finish eighth, 24 points behind third-placed Sheffield United. The year before the gap was 21.

The prospect for perceived injustice will inevitably grow but the National League, which has had a six-team play-off format since 2017-18, illustrates the difficulty of winning promotion from those extra places. Only Grimsby Town, in 2021-22, have been successful when finishing outside of the top four play-off spots.

Those clubs finishing seventh and eighth in the Championship will have it tough, but the EFL’s clubs believe this is a format that will grow the appeal of the play-offs and retain engagement through the final weeks of the season.

The idea was first proposed by former Crystal Palace and Bristol City CEO Phil Alexander as far back as 2003 but those stuck in the middle classes of the Championship, including Preston North End, have pushed to see a new, broader format introduced in the last six months.

There are risks to fixing something that was not broken, but the support from clubs was clear.
